topics.name: Data and sampling
topics.line: Statistics is <mark>using data to make a decision</mark>. You can't check everyone, so you check a slice (the sample) and let it speak for the whole group (the population).

ex.text: You want the first-serve percentage of every player on tour (the population). You can't chart every match, so you chart 200 (the sample). The sample's number is p hat; the true one is p.

qa: Describe: summarize what you have. Infer: use a sample to speak for the bigger group.
A team's average age describes. A poll predicting an election infers.
A gym surveys 150 of its 2,400 members. Population and sample?
Population: all 2,400 members. Sample: the 150 surveyed.
Random is fair to all, stratified makes every group show up, risk-based oversamples the riskiest.
An auditor looks hardest at the largest expense claims.
300 expense reports out of 50,000: how do you pick?
Stratify by amount, oversample the big claims, pick at random within each group, then reweight to real shares.
300 small claims tell you nothing about the big ones, where the money is.
No, qualitative. An average zip code means nothing.
Price, square feet and bedrooms per home?
topics.trap: A bigger sample fixes randomness, not bias. 10,000 app users who answered a survey say nothing about the ones who ignore surveys. That is a convenience sample.
topics.hook: A name is a label, a price is a number. All players on tour are the population; your 200 matches, the sample.

why.care: Every dashboard, survey and experiment is a spoonful. Whether it speaks for the pot depends on how it was taken.

topics.name: Where is the middle
topics.line: Mean is the average. Median is the middle once sorted. Mode is the most common. The big idea: one extreme number drags the mean; the median barely moves.

ex.text: Ranking points in the top 100: a few players hold huge totals, so the mean sits far above the median. For a typical top-100 player, use the median.

qa: Sorted: 0 5 7 7 11 15 22 29. Average the middle two, 7 and 11.
A few mansions blow up the mean.
The tail pulls the mean toward it.
To stop outliers pulling it: drop the top and bottom 5%, average the rest.
Useful for heavy tails, like incomes or claim sizes.
Fund A averages 6% a year, fund B 14%. Which is better?
Can't say yet. You need the risk.
The average hides how bumpy the ride is. That is the next topic.
topics.trap: Duplicates count. In 15, 7, 22, 7, 29, 11, 5, 0 the 7 appears twice, and both stay in the sorted list.
topics.hook: Mean is average salary with the boss in the room. Median is what the typical person makes. The mean chases the tail.

Short videos, then the practice set on mean and median. About 15 minutes.

Sort, take the middle; average the two middles if n is even
Most frequent value; none if all differ, bimodal if two tie
Right skew: mode < median < mean. Left skew: mean < median < mode.

why.click: The mean is where a seesaw balances. The median is the person standing in the middle of the line.
why.care: Pick the wrong one and you tell the wrong story: average pay with the CEO included describes nobody.
uses: Home prices are quoted as medians because a few mansions drag the mean up.

topics.name: How spread out is it
topics.line: Range is biggest minus smallest. Standard deviation is the typical distance from the average; in finance, risk. Empirical rule: on hill-shaped data, 68% fall within 1 SD, 95% within 2.

ex.text: Your first serve averages 115 mph with an SD of 5. About two thirds land between 110 and 120, 95% between 105 and 125. A 132 mph serve is over 3 SD out: a radar glitch, or something changed.

qa: 75 minus 12. One extreme value sets the whole range.
One outlier sets it, it ignores the middle, and it grows with n.
Why square the gaps from the mean?
A sample hugs its own average and looks too tight; n − 1 nudges the variance back up.
No. Zero only if every value is identical.
Mean 400, SD 50: where do 95% of days land?
What share of days sell more than 450?
32% sit outside 1 SD, half of them on top.
When does the empirical rule fail?
Skewed, bimodal or outlier-heavy data. Market returns have fat tails.
A quality target of about 3.4 defects per million.
That figure assumes the average drifts 1.5 SD. A perfectly centered normal process would have about 2 per billion past 6 SD.
topics.trap: Same range, different spread. 10, 50, 50, 50, 90 and 10, 10, 50, 90, 90 both span 80, but SDs of about 28 and 40. Range sees only the ends.
topics.hook: My Desk Shows Some Daily Risk: mean, distance, square, sum, divide, root. SD is how bumpy the ride is.

topics.name: Probability rules
topics.line: Or: add, then subtract the overlap. And: multiply. Given: count only inside what you were told. Mutually exclusive: can't both happen. Independent: one says nothing about the other.

ex.text: Break-point conversion is a conditional probability: P(win the point | break point). Count only the break points. Convert 20 of 50 and that is 40%.

qa: Two coins and a die: how many outcomes?
One die roll: P(not a 1 or 2)?
A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {3, 4} on one die roll. P(A or B)?
From a pack of 52 cards: P(heart or face card)?
13 + 12 − 3. Don't count the heart face cards twice.
Die roll: P(5 or 6 given the roll is above 2)?
The list shrinks to 3, 4, 5, 6, and two of those count.
60% of hotel guests use the gym, 30% the spa, 12% both. P(spa given gym)?
Two aces in a row, no replacement?
One ace and one card are gone.
Flight on time 0.85, bag arrives given on time 0.95: both?
Bag arrives given late: 0.70. Your bag arrived. Chance the flight was on time?
Add both bag-arrives branches (0.9125), then shrink.
topics.trap: Mutually exclusive events are not independent. If A happens B cannot, so knowing A changes B completely.
topics.hook: Or: two guest lists, count overlaps once. And: a combo lock, every dial must hit. Given: a filter, then count.

Multiply along a branch, add branches with the same ending

why.care: Many costly mistakes come from mixing up P(A given B) and P(B given A).

topics.name: Random variables and expected value
topics.line: A <mark>random variable</mark> is a number that depends on chance. Its <mark>expected value</mark> is the long-run average, weighted by probability. Its <mark>SD</mark> is the risk around that.

ex.text: A returns 2% or 14%, 50/50: E = 8%, σ = 6%. B: −6, 6, 12 or 24% with odds 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2: E = 10.8%, σ = 8.4%. B pays more; A has less risk per unit of return (CV 75% vs 78%).

qa: Expected value of one roll of a four-sided die (1 to 4)?
You never roll a 2.5; it is the long-run average.
Toss 3 coins, Y = number of heads. E(Y)?
Shifting every outcome moves the mean, not the spread.
A or B on expected value? On risk? On both?
topics.trap: The expected value is not the most likely outcome, and may be impossible (2.5 on a four-sided die). It is the long-run average.
topics.hook: Expected value: a bet's long-run worth. SD: how far one try can land. CV: risk per unit of reward, lower is better.

why.click: Expected value is what a bet is worth if you could make it a thousand times.
why.care: Businesses live on repeated bets: insurance, pricing, inventory. Expected value says which pay off; SD says if you survive the bad runs.

topics.name: Two variables: covariance, correlation, portfolios
topics.line: Covariance asks whether two things move together. Correlation rescales it from −1 to +1. Mix two assets and any correlation below +1 lowers the mix's risk. That is diversification.

ex.text: Asset A: E = 8%, σ = 6%. Asset B: E = 10.8%, σ = 8.4%. Covariance 12.6, so ρ = 12.6 / (6 × 8.4) = 0.25. A 50/50 mix returns 9.4% with σ = 5.74%, below either asset alone.

qa: They tend to move in the same direction
Not necessarily. Y = X² can have zero covariance and total dependence.
Zero covariance rules out only a straight-line link.
50/50 mix of A and B: expected return?
Why is the mix less risky than both assets?
ρ is only 0.25: the cross term is small, and the squared weights shrink the rest.
topics.trap: Independent means Cov = 0, but Cov = 0 does not mean independent. Y = X² is the classic catch.
topics.hook: Correlation is why you don't put all your eggs in one basket. The covariance term is where the two talk.

ρ = Cov(X, Y) / (σx σy), between −1 and 1

why.care: It is how you diversify, and how you get fooled: ice cream sales and drownings rise together because of summer.

Two columns correlated near 1 tell you the same thing twice.

topics.name: Counting and the binomial
topics.line: Repeat a yes-or-no try n independent times with the same chance p: the count of yeses is <mark>binomial</mark>, mean np, variance np(1 − p). Combinations count the ways it can happen.

ex.text: You win 60% of tiebreaks. With 3 tiebreaks in a match, P(win exactly 2) = C(3,2)(0.6)²(0.4) = 43.2%. P(win at least 1) = 1 − 0.4³ = 93.6%.

qa: Gold and silver from 5 runners: how many orders?
Pick 2 of 5 runners for a pair, order doesn't matter?
Fixed n, two outcomes, independent trials, the same p every time
20% of shoppers use a coupon, n = 8: P(exactly 2)?
A free throw goes in 70% of the time. 4 shots: P(exactly 3)?
A box of 10 phones has 3 defective. Pick 4 without replacement. P(exactly 1 defective)?
C(3, 1) × C(7, 3) / C(10, 4) = 3 × 35 / 210. This is the hypergeometric.
Same box: P(no defective in the 4)?
Without replacement, the chance changes after every draw
Binomial needs the same p each draw; fine only if you sample under about 5% of the group.
topics.trap: At least one is 1 − P(none). Adding P(1) + P(2) + … by hand is slow and invites mistakes.
topics.hook: Binomial is counting wins in a fixed number of matches, when every match is the same weighted coin.

topics.name: Poisson: counts per unit
topics.line: Poisson counts events in a fixed window when they arrive independently at a steady average rate λ. Mean and variance both equal λ. Scale λ to the window first.

ex.text: You make 3 unforced errors a set on average. P(none in a set) = e⁻³ = 5%. Over 3 sets λ = 9, so P(6 or fewer) is about 21%.

qa: A coffee shop gets 30 orders per hour. λ for 10 minutes?
Scale the rate to the window.
P(2 or more orders in 10 minutes)?
With one barista, a second order means someone waits.
Given at least one order in those 10 minutes, P(exactly one)?
P(1) / (1 − P(0)) = 5e⁻⁵ / (1 − e⁻⁵). At least one rules out zero.
A help desk gets 3 calls per hour. P(exactly 3 in one hour)?
P(4 or fewer calls in 2 hours)?
topics.trap: Forgetting to rescale λ. 3 calls an hour over 2 hours is λ = 6, not 3.
topics.hook: Poisson counts arrivals: help-desk calls, emails an hour, errors per set. Pick the window first, then count.

topics.name: The normal curve and z
topics.line: The <mark>normal</mark> is the bell. Measure in SDs from the mean, <mark>z = (y − μ) / σ</mark>, and any normal becomes the standard one. Area under it is probability.

ex.text: A cafe sells 400 coffees a day on average, SD 50. More than 475 is z = 1.5, an area of 6.7%. Stock 464 cups and you run out on about 10% of days (z = 1.28).

qa: How many cups so P(running out) ≤ 0.10?
What does a z of −2 mean?
1, half on each side of the mean
Delivery times ~ N(32, 6) minutes: P(more than 35)?
A wait is uniform from 0 to 20 minutes, not a bell. P(over 15)?
Flat, so the area is a rectangle: (20 − 15) / 20.
Mean and SD of that wait?
topics.trap: Some z tables give the area from 0 to z, not from the far left. For less than a positive z, add 0.5; Excel's NORM.S.DIST already starts from the left.
topics.hook: z is how many SDs from average. Memorize 1.28, 1.645, 1.96, 2.576 and every bell question is arithmetic.

topics.name: Sampling distributions and the CLT
topics.line: Sample means have their own distribution. The <mark>Central Limit Theorem</mark> says it is near normal for big n, centered on μ, with spread <mark>σ / √n</mark> (the standard error).

ex.text: One match's first-serve percentage bounces around. Average 36 matches and the noise shrinks 6-fold (√36). At 62% with a match SD of 6 points, the standard error is 1 point: the average almost always lands within 2 of 62.

qa: Why can we use the normal there?
Averages of many independent values come out close to normal, even when the population isn't
n over 30 is the usual rule of thumb. Very skewed data can need more.
Repair bills: mean 640, SD 480, n = 64. SE?
The total has mean 40,960 and SD 480√64 = 3,840; z = 0.792.
Depends on skew. 30 is the usual rule of thumb; a normal population works at any n.
Is a statistic a random variable?
Yes. It changes from sample to sample.
A population is 1, 2, 3 and 6. How many samples of n = 2, with replacement?
4 choices each draw. All 16 means average exactly μ = 3.
Its average over every possible sample equals the parameter
x̄ for μ, p̂ for p, and s² for σ² are all unbiased.
Why does s² divide by n − 1?
Dividing by n runs low by the factor (n − 1)/n
With n = 2 it lands on half of σ², on average. n − 1 fixes that.
x̄ or the sample median to estimate μ?
For normal data, x̄: unbiased with a smaller spread, so more efficient
It depends on the population. On skewed data the median estimates a different center.
topics.trap: Dividing σ by n instead of √n. The standard error shrinks with the square root: four times the sample only halves the noise.
topics.hook: Averaging is noise cancelling. The √n is the price: four times the data buys half the noise.

Mean p, SE = √[p(1 − p) / n], normal if np ≥ 10 and n(1 − p) ≥ 10

topics.name: Confidence intervals and sample size
topics.line: A <mark>confidence interval</mark> is your estimate plus or minus a margin: <mark>estimate ± critical value × standard error</mark>. Use z when σ is known, t when you only have s.

ex.text: You charted 20 matches: average first serve 115 mph, s = 6. 95% CI: 115 ± 2.093 × 6/√20 = 115 ± 2.8, so 112.2 to 117.8. For ±1 mph at 95%, n = (1.96 × 6 / 1)² ≈ 139 matches.

qa: 25 bottles, x̄ = 502.4 ml, σ = 5 known: 95% CI?
Same bottles: the 95% margin of error around x̄ = 502.4?
E = 1.96 × 5/√25. Intervals built this way catch μ 95% of the time; it is not a guaranteed maximum miss.
When σ is unknown and you use s. Fatter tails, bigger multiplier.
t nears z as n grows.
120 of 200 prefer the new app: 90% CI for p?
Proportion, interval width 0.06 at 95%, no prior guess: n?
Same, but p is known to sit between 0.10 and 0.20?
Use 0.20; it gives the larger n.
95% of intervals built this way catch μ. Any one interval either does or doesn't.
topics.trap: A 95% CI is not a 95% chance that μ is inside. μ is fixed; the interval moves. For sample size, width is 2E: width 0.06 means E = 0.03.
topics.hook: A confidence interval is a margin of error around your guess. More confidence widens it; more data tightens it.

topics.name: Hypothesis tests
topics.line: A hypothesis test asks: <mark>would this data be surprising if nothing were going on?</mark> Assume nothing is (H₀). A small p-value means the data would be rare, so reject H₀.

ex.text: A coffee machine should pour 250 ml. 36 cups average 247.5 ml, σ = 6. z = (247.5 − 250) / (6 / √36) = −2.5. The two-sided p-value is 0.012, under 0.05: reject H₀. It pours short.

qa: H₀ and H₁ for “the machine pours 250 ml on average”?
H₀ holds the equals sign. The claim you want evidence for goes in H₁.
Test statistic for a mean, σ known?
How many standard errors the sample landed from H₀.
That doesn't prove H₀. The data just aren't surprising enough.
16 bags: x̄ = 492 g, s = 12. Test H₀: μ = 500 against H₁: μ < 500 at 5%.
230 of 400 prefer design A. Test H₀: p = 0.5 at 5%.
Rejecting H₀ when it is true
A false alarm. Its chance is α.
Keeping H₀ when it is false
A missed signal, with chance β. Power = 1 − β; a bigger n raises it.
How does a test match a confidence interval?
A two-sided test at α rejects exactly when μ₀ is outside the (1 − α) interval
topics.trap: A p-value is not the chance H₀ is true. It is the chance of data at least this extreme under H₀. For a proportion, the SE uses p₀, not p̂.
topics.hook: Innocent until proven guilty. H₀ is the defendant; the p-value is how unlikely the evidence would be if innocent.

topics.name: Simple regression
topics.line: <mark>Regression</mark> fits the line with the smallest squared misses. <mark>Slope</mark>: how much y moves per unit of x. <mark>R²</mark>: the share of y's variation explained. <mark>t-test</mark>: does x help?

topics.name: Multiple regression
topics.line: Several x's. Each coefficient is one x's effect <mark>holding the others fixed</mark>. The <mark>F-test</mark> checks the whole model, each <mark>t-test</mark> one x. <mark>Multicollinearity</mark>: two x's saying the same thing.

tools.name: SQL
tools.blurb: Summaries, percentiles, correlation, and regression right where the data lives.
tools.intro: These assume a table orders (order_id, order_date, region, channel, amount) and a table months (ad_spend, sales). PostgreSQL, with BigQuery and Snowflake notes where they differ.
rows: COUNT(amount) skips NULLs, COUNT(*) does not. The gap is your missing values.

SELECT AVG(amount) AS mean
FROM orders;
AVG skips NULLs. Same in BigQuery and Snowflake.

SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS median
FROM orders;
Snowflake takes the same code or MEDIAN(amount). BigQuery: PERCENTILE_CONT(amount, 0.5) OVER () is a window function, so wrap it in SELECT DISTINCT.
Returns Q1, median, Q3 as an array. Same method as QUARTILE.INC in Excel. Snowflake and BigQuery take one fraction per call.
Both divide by n minus 1. STDDEV and VARIANCE mean the sample versions in all three. Use STDDEV_POP and VAR_POP for a whole population.

SELECT region,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       AVG(amount) AS mean,
       STDDEV_SAMP(amount) AS sd,
       MIN(amount) AS min,
       MAX(amount) AS max
FROM orders
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY mean DESC;
One row per region. Works as written in BigQuery and Snowflake.

SELECT region,
       SUM(amount) AS total,
       1.0 * SUM(amount) / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () AS share
FROM orders
GROUP BY region;

The window runs after GROUP BY, so SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () is the grand total. Use OVER (PARTITION BY region) with GROUP BY region, channel for each channel's share within its region. The 1.0 stops integer division in PostgreSQL.

SELECT region,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'web') AS web,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'store') AS store,
       COUNT(*) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY region;
Rows are regions, columns are channels. BigQuery: COUNTIF(channel = 'web'). Snowflake: COUNT_IF(channel = 'web'). SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'web' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) works everywhere.

SELECT CORR(ad_spend, sales) AS r
FROM months;
Pearson r. Rows with a NULL in either column are skipped. Same name in BigQuery and Snowflake.

SELECT REGR_SLOPE(sales, ad_spend) AS slope,
       REGR_INTERCEPT(sales, ad_spend) AS intercept,
       REGR_R2(sales, ad_spend) AS r_squared,
       REGR_COUNT(sales, ad_spend) AS n
FROM months;

y first, then x, as in Excel's SLOPE. Snowflake has the same functions. BigQuery has none: slope is COVAR_SAMP(ad_spend, sales) / VAR_SAMP(ad_spend), R squared is POWER(CORR(ad_spend, sales), 2), and intercept is AVG(sales) minus slope times AVG(ad_spend) over rows with both values.

SELECT order_id, amount,
       (amount - AVG(amount) OVER ())
         / STDDEV_SAMP(amount) OVER () AS z
FROM orders;
Put PARTITION BY region inside each OVER () for a z-score within each region. |z| above 3 is a common outlier flag. Same in BigQuery and Snowflake.

WITH daily AS (
  SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS sales
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY order_date
)
SELECT order_date, sales,
       AVG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date
         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg_7_day
FROM daily
ORDER BY order_date;
ROWS counts rows, so a day with no orders shortens the window; fill missing dates first if that matters. The first six rows average fewer days. Same in BigQuery and Snowflake.

BERNOULLI keeps each row with a 10% chance, so the count varies; add REPEATABLE (42) for the same sample each run. ORDER BY RANDOM() returns exactly 500 but sorts the whole table. BigQuery: ORDER BY RAND() LIMIT 500. Snowflake: SAMPLE (10) or SAMPLE (500 ROWS).
